claims.text: The starting Mg-transition-metal powder mixture has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The starting powder is elementally segregated and has an unstable microstructure prone to brittle C14 Laves phases and oxide formation.
Rapid heating to 900 °C will maximize diffusion without causing excessive elemental volatility.
Cooling at 5–10 °C/min through 700–500 °C will produce a stable, single-phase-like FCC structure or ordered domains while avoiding brittle L12 ordering and phase separation.
An argon or vacuum sintering atmosphere will prevent premature oxidation.
The proposed treatment will create a transient diffusion-controlled FCC solid solution or fine lamellar eutectic structure.
The proposed microstructure will suppress nucleation of brittle C14 Laves phases.
Maintaining homogeneous bulk composition will prevent outward Mn diffusion, Mn depletion, and the associated mechanical weakening.
Sintering at 900 °C supplies enough thermal energy for densification and homogenization of the Mg-transition-metal alloy.
A temperature of 900 °C is below the threshold for excessive Mg or Mn evaporation.
Mn-containing ternary spinel oxides form through outward diffusion and oxidation of Mn, Cr, and Fe during high-temperature air exposure.
L12 chemical ordering near 600 °C can promote planar slip, strain localization, and a ductile-to-brittle transition.
Controlled cooling through 700–500 °C will prevent brittle L12 ordered domains from forming.
At 1000 °C, insufficient oxide-formation kinetics can produce a porous, nonprotective oxide layer and exponential oxidation weight gain.
Surface enrichment in Co and Ni can create a protective noble-element barrier analogous to the FCC-L12 barrier reported for AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
The proposed process will yield greater than 95% relative density and a homogeneous microstructure free of C14 Laves phases.
The proposed process will form a continuous, nonporous Co/Ni-enriched oxide layer that lowers oxidation weight gain relative to 800 °C and 1000 °C processing.
Standard sintering at 850 °C gives incomplete densification, whereas 950 °C produces porous heterogeneous oxides and brittle intermetallic precipitates.
Density fails below 800 °C because atomic diffusion is insufficient for pore elimination.
Above 1000 °C, excessive volatility and porous oxide formation occur in the proposed Mg-transition-metal system.

contradictions.description: The proposed optimum requires controlled slow cooling at 5–10 °C/min through 700–500 °C, but the nominal optimum Batch B is rapidly quenched. The experiment therefore does not test the stated intervention.
The processing conditions specify argon or vacuum to prevent premature oxidation, whereas the experiment permits cooling in either air or inert gas, introducing an uncontrolled atmosphere difference.

The mediator permits a fine lamellar eutectic structure, which normally contains distinct phases, while the predicted outcome requires a single-phase-like homogeneous microstructure; the acceptable target structure is therefore ambiguous.
